Statement 
The Law Commission of India has submitted its 173rd report on Prevention of Terrorism Bill, 
2000. According to the Law Commission the draft bill seeks to provide Law enforcement agencies 
with suitable powers to deal effectively with the growing menace of terrorism in the country and 
also contains provisions for checking misuse of powers by the investigating agencies. 
The salient features of the Bill include a comprehensive definition of terrorist acts, provisions 
for seizure, attachment and forfeiture of proceeds of terrorism; provisions for expeditious trial by 
special courts and protection of witnesses; inve stigation by office not below the rank of Deputy 
Superintendent of Police or equivalent as also adverse inference as to accused in certain cases. 
Suitable safeguards against abuse of various provisions have been provided including confirmation 
of detention by Director General of Police an d State Review Committees within ten and thirty 
days respectively, etc. 
The Government has invited the views of the all the State Government/UT administrations on 
the various provisions of the bill. The Government will hold consultations with political parties 
and other concerned agencies/groups before taking a final view.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY  OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI I.D. SWAMI): 
(a) and (b) Home Secretary leve l talks were held in Kathma ndu from July 4.7.2000. At this 
meeting the two sides discussed modalities to e nhance cooperation in combating activities of 
terrorist, criminal and other undersirable el ements, including along th e India-Nepal border. 
Cooperation between the law enforcement agen cies of both the countries and improved 
management of the India-Nepal border were also discussed. 
(c) it was agreed to further intensify coopera tion and jointly coordina te measures, including 
stepping up vigil along the contiguous border distri cts of India and Nepal, to counter activities 
inimical to India's interests. Shared concern on  this matter was evident from the determination 
expressed by both sides to take  urgent necessary steps to control misuse of the open border 
between the two countries. It was also agreed to introduce with effect from October 1,2000, a 
"pruned down" list of photo identification documents  that would be valid for air travel by India

investment towards increasing co al production in the 24 sub-projec t under five subsidiaries i.e. 
Central coalfields Limited (CCL), Mahanadi Co alfields Limited (MCL), Western Coalfields

institutional capacity development in the project implementation, mining operations and 
management.

1181, SHRI VEDPRAKASH P. GOYAL: W ill the Minister of NON-CONVENTIONAL 
ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Solar Energy Programme is regarded- as one of the World's 
largest programme, if so, the countries which; are following the similar kind of programmes; 
(b) what 'are the highlights of the Solar Energy Programme in other countries;  
(c) if the programme. is commercially viable in  other countries, what, is the.cost incurred 
thereon; and 
(d.) what is: the difference in the level of technologies used in India and other countries? 
134 

 137
 [2 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-CONVENTIONAL  ENERGY 
SOURCES (SHRI M. KANNAPPAN): (a) and (b) Th e Indian "solar energy programme is 
regarded as one of the largest national programmes in the world in this field. Other, countries 
which have policies to support solar energy deve lopment as well as major programmes in solar 
photovoltaic and thermal technologies  include USA, Japan, Germany,  China, Australia, France, 
Netherlands, Austria, Israel, Italy and Spain. 
USA is pursuing the development and utilization of a variety of solar technologies for a large 
number of applications. A programme for the installation of 1 miltidtt solar systems on roof-tops 
of houses and Other buildings was announced in 1997. This includes solar photovoltaic systems 
for electricity generation as well as solar thermal systems for water heating. In Germany, a new 
programme for 100,000 solar roofs was launche d in 1999. About 33,000 roof-top photovoltaic; 
systems have been installed in Japan till March 2000 under its national programme. In Israel, 
legislation has made it mandatory to install sola r water heaters in several types of buildings 
including most residential utitis. Megawatt- size power plants based on solar thermal and 
photovoltaic technologies have been installed in USA. Photovotaic power plants have also been 
installed for purposes of demonstration and evalua tion in several other countries including Italy, 
Germany and Japan, Research and development is also being suppor ted in Japan, USA,.Australia 
and several European countries. 
(c) The commercial viability of any solar energy system depends on a number of factors such as 
the solar radiation level, load, c onsumption pattern and the availabili ty and cost of electricity or 
fossil fuels. The cost of electricity from solar thermal or photovoltaic sy stems is generally not 
competitive to that: generated from conventional energy sources. The megawatt-size power plants 
abroad have been built either under government-funded demonstration programmes or by 
availing of special tax benefits and other ince ntives. The solar roof programme in Japan is 
supported by government subsidies; in Germany it is supported by soft loans.and a special price 
for the electricity supplied to the grid by hous e owners. The international price for photovoltaic 
modules is around $ 4 per watt and the cost of electricity for stand-alone systems varies between 
135 

 138
RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2000] 
25 to 50 cents per kilowatt hour. However, photo voltaic power can be economical in remote and 
unelectrified areas and for small power applications, as is also the case in India. 
Solar water heating systems for household use are c onsidered to be commercially viable in most 
countries including India. The cost of a solar water hearing system of 100—120 litre capacity 
varies between $ 400—600. Industrial and institutional solar water heating systems are 
competitive only if the alternative is electricity or a high-priced fuel. 
(d) As a result of development and commercialisation efforts made during the past two decades, a 
substantial base for the manufac ture of solar photovoltaic and solar thermal products has been 
established in India. Almost the entire production of solar cells in India is based on the single 
crystal silicon technology. Technologies such  as multi-crystalline silicon, amorphous silicon and 
other thin film solar cells which account for over 60% of the world's production are not yet in 
commercial production in India. Nevertheless, so lar cells and modules made in India are being 
exported to several countries abroad. Solar collector material for thermal applications is also being 
exported from India. Several Indian companies have obtained the ISO 9000 quality certification. 
The main difference in the production of solar pr oducts in India and some other countries lies in 
the volume of production and the range of techno logies employed. Lead ing foreign companies 
have production capacities which ar e 5 to 10 times that of Indian companies. A higher level of 
automation is also seen in foreign manufacturing organizations.

(a) whether Government have received the recommendations from the institution of Engineers

Mangement Programme include ins itu soil-moisture conservation, checking of land degradation

Prone Areas Programme (DPAP), National Waters hed Development Project for Rainfed Areas

catchment of River Valley Projects & Flood Prone Rivers (RVP & FPR). Under NWDPRA.

area has been developed in the last three years.  Under IWDP, ten projects  have been sanctioned

under implementation in 16 districts. In these di stricts, 699 watershed projects covering an area 
of about 3.5 lakhs ha. are presently under impl ementation. A project under IWDP is generally 
evaluated after the release of 45% of the project costs. The task of evaluation of RVP & FPR

Compensation to Kuwait Evacuees 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, during the Iraq-Kuwait war, thousands of 
Indians working in Kuwait were evacuated. Ther eafter, a United Nations Claims Commission 
was established at Geneva to compensate the vi ctims who lost their earnings and savings due to 
the war. The victims were asked to send their claims for compensation to the United Nations 
Claims Commission (UNCC) through their respec tive Governments. In India, the Special 
Kuwait Cell coordinated and monitored the pro cessing of applications and disbursement of 
compensation. Accordingly, the Government of India, as per the decision of the UNCC, received 
applications for claims until 1991 and extended the time thereafter upto 1992. Corresponding to 
these dates, the victims had sent their applications. The Government of India notified a proforma 
in newspapers for submitting their claims. Howeve r, most of the victims of the evacuation are 
illiterate labourers and not well educated and they  could not have read the newspapers. Hence, 
they were not aware of the new procedures that have been adopted and they could not send their 
applications in the new proforma. However, the applications which were sent in plain papers 
were rejected and the victims were denied the compensation with the sole reason that they failed 
to apply in the appropriate format. All th ese victims are sufferi ng from utter poverty and 
unemployment. They are not even able to meet their needs and have two meals a day. Sir, 
thousands of workers from my district, Cuddapah,  in Andhra Pradesh are being denied of this 
compensation amount. They are unable to come over to Delhi and stay here for some days for 
this purpose. It is a costly affair to them; he nce most of the people could not come. However, 
even in the case of those people who managed to come over here, the Kuwaiti Embassy officials 
are not even giving appointments to them as their names are not included in the list of eligible 
persons for receiving the compensation. Consider ing this miserable condi tion of the people, I 
request the Government to consider their applications sympathetically and grant the 
compensation which is legitimately due to them.

Before replying to the specific points raised by  the Members of Parliament, I would like to give 
some background to the repeal of these two laws. 
The Department of Administrative Reforms had set up a Commission under the chairmanship of 
Shri P.C. Jain, in May, 1998, to review the laws and regulations, id entifying proposals for 
amendments to the existing laws and to make recommendations for repeal/amendment of the 
laws. 
The Commission has identified certain laws which are no longer relevant and, therefore, can be 
repealed. For the steel sector, the laws identified are: 
(1) The Iron & Steel Company (Taking over of Management) Act, 1972. 
(2) The Iron & Steel Companies (Amalgamation) Act, 1952. 
The Iron and Steel Companies (Amalgamation) Act, 1952 (Act No.79 of 1952) was enacted to 
amalgamate the Indian Iron & Steel Company Limited with the Steel Corporation of Bengal on 
the recommendation of the Tariff 
245 

 
RAJYA SABHA      [02 August, 2000] 
Board and the Tariff Commission. In the initia l years, after independence, when a serious 
shortage of steel was hampering the nation-building activities, it became imperative to eliminate 
duplication and waste and, ultimately, reduce the co st of production of steel. For this purpose, it 
was thought fit that the Stee! Corporation of Be ngal Limited, which had its works at Kulti, 
District Burdwan, West Bengal and the Indi an Iron and Steel Company Limited, Burnpur, 
District Burdwan, West Bengal, both of which were enga ged in the manufacture and production 
of iron and steel, should be amalgamated. The amalgamation was thought necessary to give effect 
to the schemes of the Centra! Government for expansion of the iron and steel industry and to 
make resources available for such expansion. 
The Act has now served its purpose, and no action might have been left over, which has to be 
undertaken under or in accordance with the provisions  of the said Act. It is, therefore, no more 
necessary to retain this Act on the Statute Book. 
Secondly, in accordance with the previsions of  the Indian Iron and Steel Company (Taking over 
of Management) Act, 1972 the ma nagement of Indian Iron and Steel Company was taken over 
initially for a period of two years, w.e.f. 14.7.1972, to secure its proper management. The period 
was extended for five years to co mplete restructuring and to streamline the administrative set-up 
of the Company. The said period of five years expired on 15 ,h July, 1977. Consequently, the Act 
is no longer operative. Subsequently, the Indian Iron and Steel Company (Acquisition of Shares) 
Act, 1976 was passed and the company was completely nationalised. In 1978, IISCO became a 
subsidiary of SAIL under the Public Sector iron and Steel Copmpanies (Restructuring) and 
Miscellaneous Act of 1978. Thus,. the Act, having  seized its purpose, is no longer operative and 
can be removed from the Statute book. 
As I have explained, I again state that thes e Acts have no relevance now and are in no way 
connected with the restructuring of SAIL or w ith the proposed conversion of IISCO into a joint 
venture, which is under the consideration of the Government. 
Madam, these two Acts are completely redundant now and they are no more operative. Hence, I 
request the hon. Members to support the passage of this Bill.

ship to mouth, is today wholly self-sufficient in basic foodgrains, is a tribute to our farming

a fact that there are basic structural maladies which still persist.

When India became independent, our agriculture  accounted for 50% of our national income. It 
accounted for 70% of our population, In the last 50 years, because of occupational 
diversification, the share of agriculture in the national income of our country has gone down 
from 50% to 28%. But the share of agricultural population in the lotal population has come down 
only from 70% to 65%. We, therefore, have a situation now where 50% of the national income

people dependent on agriculture has not declined as a result, The disparity in incomes between

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Incidence of killing by the Militants in Jammu and Kashmir on the intervening night of 1st 
and 2nd August, 2000 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS {SHRI L.K. ADVANI): Madam, a series of ghastly 
incidents perpetrated by militants, taking a toll of  as many as 80 lives,  have been reported from 
Jammu and Kashmir on the 
night of r: and 2'''' August, 2000. 
In the first incident, at about 18-45 hours on 1 SI August, a group of terrorists fired 
indiscriminately at Pahalgam where Amarnath Ya tris were camping. The incident took place 
across Lidder Nallah on the road leading to Aroo when terrorists fired at two Langars and CRPF 
personnel. The firing was retaliated by the CRP F. 27 persons, including two police personnel, 
have been killed and 50 injured. Two militants re sponsible for the firing were also killed on the 
spot. From them, the following recoveries have been effected: AK Rifles-2, AK Magazines- 19, 
Rifie grenades--8, Hand-grenades--2, Grenade launcher-1, Rounds-55, Transistor--1.

RAJYA SABHA      [02 August, 2000] 
In the second and third incidents, the militants had attacked two brick ki ln labour camps, one at 
Mir Bazar, Quazigund in Anantnag District, the other at Mir Nowgam (Achhabal). 19 labourers 
were killed at Mir Bazar and 7 labourers at Mir Nowgam. During the same night, in Pogal 
Paristan in Ramban area (Doda District), anot her group of militants killed 14 persons. In the 
same district in village Keyar, eight members of a village defence committee were killed by 
terrorists. The sixth incident took place at Kalaroos (Kupwara district) where five members of a 
Muslim family were massacred. 
The Stale Government has initiated precautionary and relief measures. Special Secretary in the 
Department of J and K Affairs,  along with DG, CRPF have been deputed to J and K to review 
the situation and the security arrangements along with the security forces in the field. 
Consequent on the cease-fire declaration made by the Hizbul Muzahideen and the Government's 
positive response to this offer, th ere have been reports that some of the other militant outfits, 
with a large component of foreign mercenaries,  who were unhappy about the offer of Hizbul 
Mujahideen, may create problems and escalate violence. The security forces had been alerted of 
this and have been asked to be more vigilant. II is because of this vigilance that the security 
forces had foiled an atternpt of the militants to attack the Amarnath pilgrims in a Jammu camp 
on the morning of 1st August. In this clash, one militant was killed and another injured. 
No words would be too strong to condemn these outrageous incidents of violence which are no 
doubt part of the continuing proxy war being wa ged against us by a hostile neighbour. But the 
Government feels that this latest  outburst of violence is also a determined bid by those upset at 
the prospects of peace to abort the initiative taken by the Hizbul Mujahideen last week. 
The Government is determined to continue the Amarnath Yatra with renewed security measures 
and to provide all necessary protection to the common people. Besides, the Government will 
persevere in its efforts to bring normalcy to th e State of Jammu and Ka shmir by engaging in a 
dialogue with the peace-loving people.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Resumption of Indo-Pak Talks 
* 161. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: SHRI SANTOSH 
BAGRODIA: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether United States wants India and Pakistan to resume talks and resolve the protracted 
Kashmir conflict and put back on trade the derailed Lahore peace process; and 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): (a) There is no 
US mediation on Indo-Pak talks. However, the US side has expressed a hope for the resumption of 
Indo-Pak talks. The US side has also reiterated its position, as articulated by President Clinton, namely 
urging restraint, respect for Line of Control, refraining from violence and for renewed lines of 
communication. In this context, the US side ha s urged Pakistan to create conditions for a 
meaningful dialogue to take place. The US Government has also stated publicly on a number of 
occasions, including on 7th July 2000, that it does not seek the role of a mediator between India and 
Pakistan. 
(b) Government believes that all outstanding issues between India and Pakistan should be 
resolved peacefully through bilateral dialogue. It is Government's position that Pakistan must 
create appropriate conditions for the dialogue to start, by stopping its sponsorship of and support to 
cross-border terrorism in India. 
SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Sir I would like to be educated with regard to the first line of 
the answer... 
SHRI M. VENKAIAH NAIDU: You are highly educated. 
The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Ghulam Nabi Azad.

road between the LTTE and the Sri Lankan Government.

playing a mediatory role. Like, for example, the United States expressing the hope in regard

(a) Employment of children below the age of 14, is prohibited in 13 occupations and

of children withdrawn from work, namely the scheme of National Child Labour Project 
(NCLP) and the scheme of Grant-in-aid to Voluntary Organisations. 93 NCLPS are currently 
under implementation in 11 child labour endemic states for rehabilitation of approximately 
2.00 lakh children. Government has approved continueance of the scheme of NCLP for the 
duration of the Ninth Five Year Plan and e xpansion of number of project up to 100. Under 
the Scheme of Gants-in-aid, funds are re leased to Voluntary Organisations, on the 
recommendation of the concerned State Govern ment, for taking up action oriented projects

(b) The farmers have been advised, from time to time, to adopted the 
following control measures for the prevention and protection of rust disease 
of soyabean: 
i) Summer ploughing/deep cultivation. 
ji) Soyabean crop should not be grown during rabi and summer seasons and its monoculture 
should be avoided by adopting inter-cropping. 
iii) Destruction of crop residues in rust affected soyabean fields. 
iv) All the self sown plants should be destroyed. 
v) Cultivation of rust tolerant varieties viz., PK 1024, PK 1029, JS 80-21 and Indira 
Soyabean 9. 
vi) Use of healthy seed treated with a mixture of thiram and carbendazim before 
sowing. 
vii) Prophylactic as well as curative spraying with propiconazole fungicide at flowering 
or on appearance of rust.

Madhya Pradesh under the Centrally sponsored Scheme "Oilseeds Production Programme" to the 
tune of Rs. 24.37 lakhs during 1997-98, Rs. 90.00 lakhs during 1998-99 and Rs. 104.00 lakhs 
during 1999-2000 for the control of pests and diseases in oilseed crops including soyabean. 
The State Government of Madhya Pradesh has constituted a monitoring team of scientists from 
State Agricultural Universities and Extension workers for the regular monitoring of soyabean rust 
disease.

Effect of WTO Norms on Farmers 
1242. SHRI K.C. KONDIAH: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to 
state whether Government would indicate the effect of the World Trade Organization norms 
on farmers of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
S.B.P.B.K. SATYANARAYANA RAO): The Agreement on Agriculture (AOA), which is one 
of the Agreements under the World Trade Organisation (WTO), came into force from 1st 
January, 1995. The Agreement incorporates three broad areas of commitments viz., (i) 
market access i.e. the disciplines on import restraints and import tariff, (ii) domestic 
support, i.e. subsidies by Governments to dom estic farmers, and (iii) export subsidies. 
Under market access provisions, the ACA seeks to convert all non-tariff barriers such as 
Quantitative Restrictions into tariffs. The tariff levels have been bound by India for primary 
agricultural products, processed agricultural products and edible oils, with a few exceptions, 
at 100%, 150% and 300% respectively. Therefore, import of agricultural commodities into 
India can be suitably regulated by imposing appropriate tariffs within the bound levels which, 
would protect the interest of farmers. Regarding domestic support, the ACA seeks to identify 
acceptable measures of support to farmers and to limit unacceptable trade-distorting support 
to farmers. The permissible category of support includes Government assistance on general 
services, viz., (i) research, pest and disease control, training, extension, and advisory 
services, (ii) public stock holding for food s ecurity purposes, (iii) domestic food aid, and 
(iv) direct payment to produ cers like Governmental financ ial participation in income 
insurance and safety nets, relief from natural disasters, and payments under environmental 
assistance programmes. Only the Aggregate Measure of Support (AMS) comprising the 
Product specific support and Non-Product specific support given to the agricultural sector is 
subject to reduction commitments. A maximum level of AMS upto 10% of the value of 
agricultural output for developing countries, such as India, and upto 5% for developed 
countries is exempt from reduc tion commitments. AMS given to the agricultural sector in 
India is presently below the permissible maximum level of 10% of the value of agricultural 
output and, therefore, India is under no oblig ation to reduce domestic support rendered to 
the agricultural sector. India has no reducti on commitments under export subsidies since no 
such subsidies are provided by the Government. 
Food security concerns are central to the ag ricultural policy of India and the export-
import policy of agricultural products is governed principally by such concerns, the need to 
maximise farmer's income and foreign exchange

products, while at the same time protect ing, and providing avenues for rural

estimates put energy output of draught animals as equivalent of 30,000 megawatt and area cultivated

diesel as 22.75 million tones per year through use of animal power. In terms of originating traffic,

purposes. Preventing their slaughter is not contemplated at this stage. However, several 
State Government enacted legi slation relating to prevention of slaughter of cow and its 
progeny. The States of Arunachal Pradesh, Kerala, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and 
Tripura as well as Union Territory of Lakshw adeep do not have any legislation in this

1288. SHRI K.M. KHAN: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state:

regard; and

Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan and Bihar during the last three years in these connections? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM CHAUHAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The need for further streamlining the Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) 
with focus on better targetisation and increasing the allocation of foodgrains to families below 
Poverty Line (BPL) had been engaging the attention of Government for some time. 
Accordingly the following modifi cations with effect from 1.4. 2000 have been effected in 
the TPDS for better targetising the food s ubsidy towards enhancing the food security for 
BPL families:— 
(i) The quantity of foodgrains for BPL families under the TPDS has been doubled 
from the existing 10 Kg. per month per family to 20 kg. per month per fami)y 
at 50% of the economic cost; 
(ii) The allocation for Above Poverty Line (APL) families has been maintained at 
the same level as fixed at the time of introduction of TPDS in June, 1997 but 
the Central Issue Price (CIP) has been fixed at Economic Cost; 
(iii) Additional quantities of wheat and rice over and above the normal monthly 
allocation, if demanded by the States/UTs are also considered subject to 
availability and at economic cost. 
These measures have resulted in a transfer of subsidy from APL to BPL population to 
the extent of Rs. 2217 crores i.e. BPL subsid y in the earlier scheme  was Rs. 5439 crores 
whereas in the modified scheme it is Rs. 7656

the earlier dispensation, there was subsidy for APL also. The revision in the prices

resources to the poor.

poverty alleviation, generation of employment, nutrition and health care etc. which 
contribute to enhancement of food security in the country.

RESOLUTION 
In order to reduce storage and transit losses of foodgrains at farm and commercial 
level, to modernise the system  of handling, storage and transportation of the foodgrains 
procured by the Food Corporation of India (FCI) and to bring in additionallity of resources 
through private sector involvement, the-Gove rnment has approved a National Policy on 
Handling, Storage and Transportation of Foodgrains, details of which are given below:— 
1. Objectives of the Policy 
The main objectives of the policy are: 
(i)    to reduce storage and transit losses at farm level where about 70% of the 
total foodgrains production is retained and 
91 

RAJYA SABHA                      [3rd August, 2000] 
consumed and also to encourage the farmers to adopt scientific storage 
methods. 
(ii) to modernise the system of hand ling, storage and transportation of the 
foodgrains procured by Food Corporation of India (FCI).  
(iii) t o  h ar n es s  ef f o r t s  an d  r es o u r ces  o f  public and private sectors, both domestic 
and foreign, to build and operate infrastructure for introduction of bulk handling, 
storage and transportation of foodgrains in the country. 
2. Policy for house-hold storage 
 Since the house-hold sector retains about 70% of the total production and 
substantial quantities of foodgrains are wasted due to improper storage at 
farm level, the major focus is on the improvement of storage standards at 
farm level. Presently, the only scheme targeting this need is the Save Grain 
Campaign, which popularises  the use of metallic and non-metallic storage 
structures and educates the farmer s about the adoption of s c i e n t i f i c  
storage methods. The scheme also aims at development/improvement of 
non-metallic traditional storage structures. 
 In order to have greater success in this area, following initiatives have been 
approved:— 
(i) introduction of a scheme to encourage use of metal bins as well as non-
mettalic storage structures at indivi dual farm level and construction of 
RCC bins at community level with appropriate financial incentives. 
(ii) strengthening of the existing research and training components of 
t he Save Grain Camp aign Scheme for scientific storage and 
preservation of foodgrains and their propagation among farmers. 
3. Modernisation and Upgradat ion of Bulk Grain Handling 
Infrastructure 
3.1 In order to reduce storage losses, it is  necessary to develop and modernise the 
infrastructure for integrated bulk handling, storage and transportation in India. The 
thrust of the policy should be:— 
(i)    encouragement of mechanical harvesting, cleaning and drying at farm and 
mandi level. 
92 

[3rd August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) transportation of grains from farm to silos by specially designed trucks. 
(iii) construction of a chain of silos at procurement as well as distribution points. 
(iv) transportation of grain from silos to railhead and thereafter to pre-determined 
destinations by specially designed trucks/fail wagons (with top filling and 
bottom discharge mechanism) dedicated trains. 
(v)    declaration of foodgrains storage as infrastructure. 
 For storage of foodgrains procured by the FCI, integrated bulk handling facilities with silos 
of large capacity for wheat along with tes ting facilities for quality control would be 
created at about 20 identified central locations in producing and consuming areas as 
well as a few port towns. These facilities, including the infrastructure for bulk 
transportation to these centres, will be created and maintained in the private sector under 
the overall co-ordination of the FCI. The design of special top filling and bottom 
discharge wagons would be decided the consultation with the Ministry of Railways. 
The Ministry of Railways will also be consulted while deciding the locations and the 
circuits where these wagons would ply. FCI will guarantee utilisation of these facilities 
to the extent of 100% for the first ten years and 75% for the next ten years. From these 
points, secondary transportation of foodgrains would be made in bag form to about 500 
godowns in important central locations in different States to be owned and 
maintained by the FCI. Further transportation to the consuming centres for retail distribution 
under the Public Distribution System will be carried out by the State Governments. 
 The private sector will be encouraged to build storage capacities in which they will 
store and maintain foodgrains procured by the Government agencies, for which 
they will be entitled to storage charges. 
 The private sector participation should be sought and encouraged for development of 
infrastructure of the integrated bulk handling, storage and transportation through— 
(i) measures such as Build-Own-Opera te-Transfer (BOOT), Build-Own-Lease-
Transfer (BOLT), Build-Own-Operate(BOO), Lease-Develop-
Operate(LDO), Joint Ventures etc. 
93 

RAJYA SABHA                    [3rd August, 2000] 
(ii)    generation of funds through public issues by private enterprises. 
(iii)    automatic approval for Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) upto 100%. 
(iv)    loans from financial institutions, NABARD, external commercial borrowings. 
(v)    fiscal incentives as given below: 
 100% deduction in profit for the purpose of Income Tax for the first five 
years and 30% deduction in profit for the next five years. 
 deduction of 40% of the profits derived by financial institutions financing 
such projects, as provided to fi nancial corporations engaged, inter-alia, in 
providing long term finance for agricultural development. 
 customs duty exemption for items not ma nufactured in India, on a case-to-
case basis, subject to a list of such equipment being submitted in advance. 
4. Development of Infrastructure Facilities at Ports 
India has been traditionally the importer of foodgrains and, therefore, the infrastructure 
facilities available at the ports are basica lly meant for unloading operations and not for 
exports. For unloading operations, ship gears are normally used. Even the latest 
mechanised facilities at Jawaharlal Nehru Po rt, Navi Mumbai have been designed for 
import purposes only. There is also lack of general cargo berths at the major ports and 
very limited warehousing facilities are availabl e for the storage of foodgrains at ports. 
For creating the proper port facilities for foodgrains meant for export in due course, the 
infrastructure facilities would have to be  developed for which following actions are 
required: 
(i) identification of ports to be developed for purposes of export of foodgrains. The 
distribution of foodgrains traffic may spread over to the non-traditional ports which 
have spare capacity like New Mangalore and Cochin ports; 
(ii) development of more general cargo berths at the ports through ports, own 
investment/private participation; 
94 

[3rd August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(iii) water front/berths can be leased to the users who may be encouraged to put 
up their own facilities; and 
(iv) development of dedicated modern f oodgrains handling faci lities at selected 
ports. 
5. Role of the Central Government 
The Central Government would: 
 facilitate speedy clearance of projects concerning development of 
infrastructure for bulk handling, transportation and storage of foodgrains by 
setting up an Approval Board competent to take final decision; 
 enter into bilateral agreem ents with other countries/ international agencies 
for p r o v i d i n g  technical/financial assistance; 
 take necessary legislative/administrative measures for removing impediments 
with regard to stock control Orders /movement control Orders framed by 
various State Governments; 
 utilize the services of an existing independent regulatory mechanism for 
fixing/regulating tariff for various ope rations, such as cleaning, drying, 
storage, transportation etc.; 
 make available facilities of the Railways for bulk transporatation; 
 promote negotiable Ware house Receipt System by which farmers could 
hold their grains back from market and meet their working capital/short 
term requirement by borrowing from banks against these receipts; and 
 promote research for development of alternate storage technologies like 
Vacuum Process Storage (VPS) technology which would ensure longer 
shelf life of foodgrains and help export of foodgrains in vacuum packs. 
6. Role of the State Government 
The State Government would help in: 
(a)    acquisition of land required for various projects as for public purpose; and 
95 

RAJYA SABHA                        [3rd August, 2000] 
(b)    making available other facilities such as water, power, road, etc.

Statement-II 
Main Recommendations of the Working Group on Information Technology 
for Masses 
The Working Group on "IT for Masses", has recommended that 
 Government should facilitate establishment of onc million IT Kiosks, with 
useful Government and private content available on revenue sharing basis. 
 Take up immediate programme to estab lish IT education infrastructure in 
60,000 schools. 
 Launch Mass Awareness Campaign through IT Yatras and other programmes. 
 Set up specific time table for Web-enabled Citizen Oriented Government 
Services; and 
 Set up 'IT Mission" for 5 years to carry out this focussed programme. 
The theme on which the report revolves, is that IT can be effective tool of 
"Empowering people" in real sense. To achieve this objective, it is necessary 
121 

RAJYA SABHA                                 [3rd August, 2000] 
to provide "Easy Access at affordable rates". "1 million IT Kiosk by 2005" will be the model to 
reach out to the masses who can not afford PC and Internet. The theme of the Working Group 
emphasizes that spread of IT is possible if IT infrastructure penetrates to schools, at the earliest. 
Government must develop Web-centric Citizen Oriented applications and make it available on 
Public Access System. Mass awareness Campaign is needed to make public aware of the immense 
benefits of the IT revolution. All these efforts will ensure "Digital Unite" rather than "Digital 
Divide". 
The other major recommendations are, mat mile connectivity should be franchised on 
revenue sharing model, private E-Com information infrastructures should be allowed CUG 
status, promote indigenous technology for low cost Internet access devices and Indian language 
development, Right of Way should be granted cable operators also. On E-Governance front the 
Working Group has recommended that Centre and States should prepare five year IT Plans and 
keep 5% of the budget for this which will ensure more productive and efficient use of remaining 
95% of the budget; take immediate steps for sensitization of decision makers, standardize formats 
and procedures by setting up Administrative Re-engineering Commission; make sure that IT 
infrastructure is in place at working level staff by 200.1 and set up time table for citizen oriented 
applications to go on Web. 
The Group has recommended that 60,000 schools in 6000 blocks, should have minimum lOPC 
infrasturcture  in place in five year time frame. This is possible through joint efforts of Centre and State 
Governments, industry, NGOs, donors, NRIs and schools themselves. Central Government can either provide 
10% of the cost or provide free Internet, useful appliances, CDs and Teachers training. 
The Group has also suggested a new scheme  called "Antyodaya Computer Literacy 
Programme". One lakh youths from SC/ST/BPL will be provided IT foundation course in this 
scheme every year for next five years. 
In a novel scheme, the Woking Group has suggested that IT YATRA should be organised 
between January, 2001 to February, 2001 from four comers of the country, demonstrating "benefits of 
IT in empowering people". Various competitions and National IT talent search are other 
programmes of the recommended package. 
The Group has recommended setting up of "IT Mission" for focussed follow up on all 
these measures for the period of next five years.

Statement 
Text of the speech made by Minister of Labour, Andhra Pradesh In 1LC in June, 
2000. 
I am grateful to the president for giving me this opportunity to lend the support of our 
country to the cause of health and safety of agricultural workers. As you may know, we have 
the largest population of agricultural workers in our country, approximately 150 million, and we 
are committed as a nation and as a Government to their welfare, health and safety. The initiative 
taken by the ILO 
135 

RAJYA SABHA                            [3rd August, 2000] 
to formulate international instruments, that is a convention supplemented by a 
Recommendation, on health and safety for agricultural workers is both timely and 
commendable. Agricultural work activities range over a very large spectrum, from the most 
modern farms and plantations to those undertak en by small, medium-sized and marginal 
farmers, and even sharecroppers, squatters and indigenous people. The ILO has estimated 
that there are about 1.3 billion workers enga ged in agricultural production worldwide, and 
there are about 170,000 fatal workplace casualties among such workers annually. This 
sector is also assessed as one of the thre e most accident-prone, along with mining and 
construction. Therefore, the need to provide pr otection and safety to such workers is self-
evident. In developing countries, most of th e holdings are small and medium-sized, and 
often the whole family is engaged in agricu ltural activities. Generally, such workers are 
poor, have little education, suffer from malnutrition, and are v i ct ims of chronic ill health. 
They also lack access to social and health care services. Many of them migrate from poor 
environmentaly and economically  disadvantaged regions to seek job opportunities in more 
prosperous ones. Some of them migrate through contractors. All of them are exposed to 
various kinds of trauma, such as social excl usion and exploitation by ruthless employers. 
In India, we have about 150 million agricult ural workers who generally belong to the 
poorest and the most disadvantaged strata of society. Their working and l ivi ng  conditions 
are covered under various labour laws such as the Workers' Compensation Act, 1923, the 
Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Plantations Labour Act, 1951,  the Employment Provident 
Fund and Miscellaneous Provisi ons Act, 1952, the Insecticides Act, 1968, the labour 
C o n t r a c t  Regulation a n d  Abolition A c t ,  1 9 7 0 ,  t h e  E q u a l  R e m u n e r a t i o n s  A c t ,  1976, the 
Interstate Migrant Workers Act, 1979, the Dangerous Missions Regulations Act, 1983 and 
the Child Labour Prohibition Abolition Act, 1983, etc. 
Many of these laws have provisions for the health and safety of agricultural 
workers,but clearly much more needs to be done. With a view to providing social protection 
and welfare measures for agricultural workers in India, we have been engaged for some time 
now in the task of formulating a comprehensive law for them. We therefore welcome this 
step taken by the ILO. The provisions of the ILO instrument are sufficiently 
comprehensive, and when implemented will no doubt bring much relief to large numbers of 
workers worldwide, as indeed it will for the m ajority of workers of rural India. I t  is  th er ef or e 
a matter of satisfaction that the Committee on Safety and Health in Agriculture has concluded 
its first discussion and has come out with draft conclusions on the subject. 
136 

[3rd August, 2000] RAJYA  SABHA 
While recognizing that some of t h e  st andards may pose difficulties for some 
developing countries wishing to ratify such a convention, we still strongly s upport this 
proposal, which will do much to ensure a heal thy and safe workplace in the agricultural 
sector.

1360. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to state:

(b) to (d) The decision to set up the Second National Commission on Labour was

Statement 
Terms of Reference of the Second National Commission on Labour 
The terms of reference of the Sec ond National Commission on Labour are as 
under:— 
(i) to suggest rationalisation of existing laws relating to labour in the organised 
sector; and 
(ii) to suggest an umbrella legislation for ensuring a minimum level of protection to 
the workers in the un-organised sectors. 
163 

RAJYA SABHA                             [3rd August, 2000] 
While drafting the framework for the above, the Commission may take into account the 
following:— 
(i) follow-up implications of the reco mmendations made by the Commission set 
up in May 1998 for review of various administrative laws governing industry; 
(ii) the emerging economic environment involving rapid technological changes requiring 
response in terms of change in methods, timings and c onditions of work in 
industry, trade and services, globalisation of economy, liberalisation of trade and 
industry and emphasis on international compet itiveness and the need for 
bringing the existing laws in tunc with the future labour market needs and demands: 
(iii) the minimum level of labour protection and welfare measures and the basic 
institutional framework for ensuring the same in a manner which is conducive to 
a flexible labour market and adjustments necessary for furthering technological 
change and economic growth; and 
(iv) improving the effectiveness of measures relating to social security, occupational 
health and safety, minimum wages and linkage of wages with productivity and in 
particular the safeguards and facilities required for women and handicapped 
persons in employment.

time-found fiscal reform programmes with the help of medium term assistance 
of Rs 1000 crores extended by the Govern ment of India from the Fiscal Reform 
Facility. The corrective measures identified for implementation fall under 
four broad categories:— 
 Reduction of Revenue Deficit 
 Disinvestment programmes in non-essential sectors. 
 Restructuring of government through decentralisation aimed at promoting greater 
efficiency in planning and expenditure. 
 Institutional reform to promote more effective regulation, lower transaction costs, 
and increase efficiency in public activities and in the economy in general.

Government of Uttar Pradesh:— 
Measures already taken to reduce revenue deficit include (i) reduction of non-
plan revenue expenditure (through baa on foreign travel, ban on air travel by 
certain categories of staff, abolition of leave encashment facility for Class I ft II 
employees, non-expansion of educational institutions on the grant-in-aid list and 
ban on providing loan/share capital to Public Sector Undertakings), (ii) Increase 
in tax revenue (through levy of new entry tax, rationalisation of the tax structure 
and intensive drive to recover arrears of government dues and arrest leakages of 
revenues), (Hi) increase in non-tax revenue (through revision of fees of 
engineering colleges ft hospital rates and revision of Nazul rates), (iv) revision of 
user charges for various economic and social services.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Reported Leptospirosis outbreak in Maharashtra and Gujarat 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. THAKUR): 
Recently, practitioners from North-west of Mumbai and adjacent area from Thane District 
(Malad-Virar) as weff as from Central part of Thane district (Kalyan),. reported increase in 
fever with a typical feature like bleeding and hepato-renal failure with involvement of lungs 
and high mortality. The practitioners from Mumbai suspecte'd Leptospirosis. Immediately 
concerned officers from the State visited the places and carried out the basic investigation, 
including entomological studies and gave directions regarding control. 
To meet the crisis a meeting of officers from Health Services, Medical Education 
and Research and Municipal Corporations wa s convened in the Directorate of Health 
Services, Mumbai on 29 th July, 2000. The possibilities  considered   for   increased  fever   
cases   were   Leptospirosis,

treatment were given al! over the State. Medical Teams were formed to assess the extent of 
the outbreak, which have been functioning in th e field. The State level rapid response team 
alongwith team from National Institute of Virology. Pune has already carried out 
investigations. For confirmation of Leptospiro sis and investigating the outbreak, a team 
from (he fndian Council of Medical Research has also reached Mumbai.

Leptospirosis is a zoonotic bacterial diseas e caused by leptospires of which there 
are many sero-groups and serovars. A number of leptospirosis outbreaks have been reported 
in India in the past namely; Andaman & Nicobar Islands. Gujarat, Karnataka, Kerala and 
Tamil Nadu. It causes a wide variety of clin ical manifestations. Jaundice and haemorrhagic 
manifestations are present in typical cases. At times cases may be misdiagnosed as viral 
fever, dengue haemorrhagic fever, malaria, etc. 
Mode of transmission 
Contact with skin (with cuts and bruises) and mucous membrane with water soil 
or vegetation contaminated with urine of infected animals like rats, pigs, cattle, dogs, etc.   
leads to infection in man,

Treatment and Prevention 
Specific treatment with anti-microbials is effective if started early in the course of illness. 
Penicillin, cephalosporins, doxycycline, erythromycin are all effective. Preventive measures 
includes elimination or minimization of human contact with contaminated water, soil or 
vegetation. Proper protective clothing such as boots and gloves are recommended in areas 
where risk is perceived to be high. 
Diagnosis is based on serological tests an d Isolation of leptosplrosis from the blood 
and urine. Facilities for serological disease are available with NICD, MICR and several medical 
institutions including State Government hospitals and medical colleges. 
On the direction of the Director General, Indian Council of Medical Research 
(ICMR), Director, Regional Medical Research Centre, Port Blair has reached Mumbai to help in 
carrying out investigations to confirm the di agnosis. A team from National Institute of 
Communicable Diseases has also been deputed to assist the State Health Authorities in 
containment and investigation. 
The Central Government is seized of  the matter and dosely monitoring the 
situation. 
All Central assistance required and considered necessary will be provided to the State 
Government.

Population Growth 
*184. SHRI RAJU PARMAR:  
SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have conducted any study to find out the causes of failure 
of population control drive, despite plan ned programmes involvi ng huge expenditure 
both by the Central and State Governments, besides NGOs and individuals; 
(b) if so, the outcome thereof; and 
(c) what effective steps are contemplated to ensure perceptible control of 
population growth as the country enters the 21st Century? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. THAKUR): 
(a) and (b) The results of the Sample Registration System reveal that the Birth Rate, in 
the country had declined to 26.5 in 1998 fro m 40.8 in 1951; the total Fertility Rate, 
which was 6.0 in 1951 declined to 3.3 in  1997 and the natural growth rate of 
population has come down to 1.75% during the year 1998. This decline in birth rate 
has been observed despite death rate declining more sharply and life expectancy at 
birth increasing almost to double since independence due to improved health services 
in the country. 
Currently the population is growing rapidl y due to: (i) large size of the population 
in the reproductive age group (estimated cont ribution 60%); (ii) higher fertility due to 
unmet needs to contraception (estimated contribution 20%); and (iii) high wanted 
fertility due to prevailing hi gh infant mortality rate (estimated contribution about 
20%). 
(c) In order to speed up the efforts of population stabi lization in the country, 
Government has adopted the National Popul ation Policy, 2000 in February 2000, 
which provides a holistic approach to the programme. It enumerates various 
Strategies and Action Plan to achieve i mmediate, medium and long-term objectives. 
The Policy 
28 

[4 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
lists national socio-demographic goals for 2010 leading to population stabilization by 
2045.

THE MINISTER OF THE STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI):  (a) and (b) India ratified the 
Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer on June 19, 1991 and the 
Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer on September 17, 
1992. The Ozone Depleting Substances (Reg ulation and Control) Rules, 2000 have 
been notified in the Gazette of India on 19t h July, 2000. Important provisions of these 
Rules are given as under: 
(i) The Rules prohibit the use of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) in manufacturing 
various products beyond 1.1.2003 except for use in metered dose inhaler and 
other medical uses. Simila rly use of balloons are prohibited after 1.1.2001 
except for essential use. Other Ozone Depleting Substances (ODS) such as

methyl bromide has been allowe d upto 1.1,2015. Since hydrochloro-
florocarbons (HCFCs) are used as inte rim substitute to re place CFCs these 
are allowed to be used upto 1.1.2040. 
(ii) It regulates production of Ozone Depleting Substances. They are to be phased 
out by 2010. 
(iii) The Rules have provisions for compulsory registration of ODS producers, 
manufacturers of ODS based products, importers, exporters stockist and 
sellers, and the same provision is appl icable to manufacturers, importers and 
exporters of compressors. 
(iv) The Rules provide for maintaining records and filing of periodic reports for 
monitoring production and use of ODS. 
(v) It also mandates that enterprises ho w have received financial assistance from 
Multilateral Fund have to register the da te of completion of their project and 
to declare that the equipment used for ODS has been destroyed. 
(vi) It prohibits creation of new capacity or expansion of capacity of manufacturing 
facilities of ODS and ODS based equipment.

Protocol. 
(ix) Authority has been specified to issue licence for all imports and exports of 
ODS and products containing ODS. 
(c) The gradual phaseout strategy for production of CFCs in India was 
approved by the Executive Committee of the Montreal Protocol in November, 1999. 
The draft notification public problished in April 1998 has been updated by 
incorporating the provisions to regulate and control the production of CFCs. The 
revised draft rules were published in the Gazette of India 25th Jan., 2000 for

National programmes for quality education 
1487. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the national programmes for ensuring quality education through improvement 
of teaching methods, teachers training and improvement of curriculum; 
(b) the State-wise target se t and status of allocate d amount sanctioned on each 
programme; and 
(c) the details of proposals received fro m Assam during last three years under 
Centrally sponsored scheme of Restruct uring and Reorganisation of Teachers 
Education (CTE) and sanctiona l status of each, including the proposal of Lakhimpur 
Post Graduate Training College? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOU RCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) and (b) A Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Restructuring and 
Reorganisation of Teacher Education was started in 1987-88 to create an academic and 
technical resource base for orientation training and continuous upgradation of 
knowledge, competence and pedagogical skills of school teachers. The scheme 
envisages setting up of District  Institutes of Education & Training (DIETs), Colleges 
of Teacher Education (CTEs) and Institutes of Advanced Studies in Education 
(IASEs) to provide resource support to elementary, secondary and adult education. No 
State-wise targets are set. However, 50 DIETs, 100 CTEs and 40 IASEs are proposed 
to be set up under the scheme till the end or IX Plan. So far 454 DIETs, 76 CTEs and 
34 IASEs have been sanctioned. List of sanctioned projects, State and UT—wise, and 
amount allocated during the last three years is given in Statement-I. 
National Council for Education Research & Training (NCERT) organises inservice 
programmes for the faculty of DIETs, C TEs, IASEs  and  State Councils of 
Educational  Research  & Training 
122

(SCERTs) for ensuring quality education th rough teacher training and improvement 
of teaching methods and curriculum. NCERT has also been organizing Special 
Orientation Programme for Primary School Teachers (SOPT) of the country to 
enhance the classroom practices, Minimum Levels of Learning (MLLs) and training 
in equipment and apparatus provided in the Operation Blackboard Scheme. Till now 
about 14,23,229 teachers have been trained in this programme. 
University Grants Commission (UGC) also strives to maintain high standards of 
teaching in universities and colleges through various programmes/schemes such as 
Academic Staff Colleges (ASCs), refresher courses conducted by select 
universities/special institutions, panels of experts in various subjects, curriculum 
development centres, Special Assistance Programmes for improvement of teaching 
and research, etc. Grants of Rs. 1485.53 lakhs under the programme of Academic Staff 
Colleges and Rs. 33.16 lakh for work of subject panels were released during 1998-99. 
Also, the All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) is extending the 
Quality Improvement Programme (QIP) for full time teachers of approved degree 
level technical education institutions so that the existing t eachers may enhance their 
professional qualification and competence. Details of Budget Allocation/Expenditure 
under the programme during the last three years is given in Annexure-II. 
Besides, four Technical Teacher's Training Institutes (TTTIs) located at Calcutta, 
Chennai, Chandigarh and Bhopal are Resource Ins titutes for quality improvement of 
polytechnic education. These Institutes are engaged in training of teachers of 
polytechnics through long, modular and shor t courses, prepare and supply learning 
resource materials to polytechnics and, assist State Councils and other academic bodies 
regarding curriculum development, admissi on procedure and examination reforms.

1493. SHRI BIRABHADRA SINGH: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether literacy rate among scheduled castes and scheduled tribes is far below 
the national rate; 
(b) if so, the action being taken to im prove the literacy rate among these 
communities, the total amount of funds earmarked for the purpose in the Eight, 
(1992—1997) and Ninth Five Year Plans (1997—2002), as compared to the total 
Plan Outlays of the Ministry of HRD, both in actual and percentage figures; and 
(c) the total funds earmarked for the Education Sector in both the Five Year Plans 
and out of that the amount of funds exclusively earmarked for educational 
empowerment of SC/STs? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOU RCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) Yes, Sir. The NSSO Survey (53rd Round) shows that the 
general literacy rate for India has moved up to 62%. However this survey does not 
give the disaggregated figures for SCs/STs. The literacy rate of Scheduled Castes and 
Scheduled Tribes, in the country, as per 1991 Census was 37.41% and 29.60% 
respectively, as compared to the general literacy rate of 52.21%. 
(b) and (c) In the literacy campaigns th e Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes 
are specially targeted. These campaigns reach  out to areas of the country which are 
most backward, illiterate and poverty st ricken. Areas of Scheduled Caste and 
Scheduled Tribe concentration are covered on a priority basis and these groups are 
invariably accessed to a greater degree. 
The Specific steps being taken by the Government to improve literacy among 
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes include; 
131 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2000] 
Funding of Literacy projects by Central a nd State Governments in the ratio of 4:1 
for Tribal districts as against 2:1 for other areas; opening of primary schools on 
priority basis; development of instructional material in tribal languages at the initial 
stages; establishment of hostels, residen tial schools, provision of scholarships and 
freeships; launching of District Primary E ducation Programme in backward districts 
with low female literacy rates. 
The three pronged strategy for increasing literacy in the country consists of; 
(i) Universalisation of Elementary Education; 
(ii) Non-Formal Education for School Drop-Outs in the age group of 9-14 years 
and; 
(iii) Literacy Campaigns & Continuing Education Programme of the National 
Literacy Mission for adult learners.

Rate of royalty for lignite in Gujarat 
1506. SHRI ANANTRAY DEVS HANKER DAVE: Will the Minister of MINES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Gujarat Government has represented to streamline the existing 
system of departmentally fixing the rates of royalty; 
(b) whether it has proposed to set up any statutory body of experts for revision of 
royalty rates; 
(c) whether any decision has been taken to review the royalty of lignite every 
three years; 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS, SPORTS AND MINES (SHRI 
SUKHDEV SINGH DHINDSA): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. Conventionally a Study Group 
is constituted in the Department/ Ministry concerned to review the rates of royalty on 
major minerals which comprises representati ves of State Governments, the Industry, 
the technical institutions and other concerned Ministries/ Departments. The Study 
Group makes recommendations about the rates of royalty after holding broad-based 
consultations which are considered by the Government and final revision of the rates 
of royalty is notified in the gazette. There is no proposal to set up any statutory body of 
experts for revision of royalty rates. 
(c) to (e) Ministry of Coal has informed that they had set up a Study Group on 
16.3.95 to consider the revision of royalt y rate of lignite. The Study Group in its 
recommendations made on 14.9.97 suggested that the rate of royalty on lignite should 
be linked with that of coal. Based on th e recommendations of the Study Group, the 
Ministry of Coal is considering to enha nce the rate of royalty on lignite to a 
reasonable level. No periodici ty of revision of royalty ra tes on minerals including 
lignite has been laid down in law. The proviso to section 9(3) of the Mines and 
Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act, 1957 stipulates that no enhancement of 
royalty rate on minerals can be done more than once during any period of three years.

1508. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the major ongoing projects in the mining sector and the order of 
investment proposed thereon, projectwise; 
(b) whether Government have in itiated reform process in Mines sector to attract

and

THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS, SPORTS AND MINES (SHRI 
SUKHDEV SINGH DHINDSA): (a) In the public sector, the National Aluminium 
Company Limited (NALCO) has undertaken the expansion of the capacity of Bauxite 
Mines from 2.4 Million Tonnes Per year (MTP Y) to 4.8 MTPY and that of Alumina 
Refinery from 0.8 MTPY to 1.575 MTPY at  Damanjodi at an investment of Rs. 
1664.60 crores. NALCO has also undertaken the expansion of capacity of Aluminium 
Smelter from the existing 2,30,000 Tonnes Pe r year (TPY) to 3,45,000 TPY and that 
Captive Power Plant from 720 MW to 840 MW at Angul for an investment of Rs. 
2062 crores. Bharat Aluminium Company Lim ited, also in the public sector, has 
undertaken the installation 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2000] 
of a New Cold Rolling Mill with a capacity of 40000 TPY alongwith associated facilities at 
Korba Aluminium Complex at an investment of Rs. 157.50 crores. 
(b) to (e) The Government allows foreign equity holding upto 100%, on the 
automatic route for all minerals (except diamonds and precious stones). This covers 
exploration, mining, mineral processing and metallurgy. In  the case of diamonds and 
precious stones, foreign equity upto 74% is allowed on the automatic route for both 
exploration and mining operations. For proposals seeking higher than 74% foreign 
equity, the cases go to the Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) for 
approval. The Mines & Minerals [Development & Regulation] Act, 1957 has also 
been suitably amended and further powers have been delegated to the State 
Governments. These recent changes in the Act are expected to streamline the 
procedure for obtaining mineral concessions from the State Governments. They also 
provide adequate security of tenure to the investors. It is expected that these policy 
changes will lead to a faster growth and development of the Indian mineral sector, and 
also application of world class mining technology. 
The FIPB, in consultation with the Minist ry of Mines, has so far approved 65 
proposals of Foreign Direct Investment in the mining sector. The likely investment in 
these cases will be about Rs. 3650 crores . Most of these proposals speak only about 
their investment plans and do not specify the area where they would like to operate. It 
is not mandatory for an applicant company to specify the area-State where they would 
like to operate. The approval granted by FIPB is only for foreign equity participation 
in a Company incorporated in India. After obtaining FIPB approval these companies 
are required to apply to the concerned State Government, which are the owners of 
minerals in their respective territorial ju risdictions, for mineral concessions. Before 
granting the mineral concessions, State G overnments need the prior approval of the 
Central Government only in respect of minerals in the First Schedule of the Mines & 
Minerals [Development & Regulation] Act, 1957. The Central Government does not 
keep data of mineral concessions granted by State Governments.

Checking Crimes in Trains 
tl524. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR; Will the Mi nister of RAILWAYS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether his Ministry has prepared any action-plan to check crimes and 
robberies in trains; 
(b) if so, whether the Ministry has made any efforts for a joint action to be taken 
by Railway Protection Force and Government Railway Police under the strategy for 
checking crime and sabotage in the train; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI 
DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) 'Policing' being a state subject under the Constitutional of 
India, prevention of crime in the runni ng trains and Railway premises is the 
constitutional responsibility of the State Gove rnment concerned which they discharge 
through their Government Railway Police (GRP). The Railway administration, on 
their part, maintains close liaison and c oordination with the State Government and 
renders necessary assistance to them to contain crime on railways. 
The Ministry of Home Affairs had conve ned a meeting on 8-4-1996, to review the 
measures taken to prevent crime, robbery and docoity in the trains. Ministry of 
Railways has suggested an 'Actional Plan' in the meeting. This Actional Plan and other 
suggestion were communicated to the State Governments for taking appropriate 
action. 
(b) and (c) The Ministry of Railways had subsequently called a joint meeting of 
Chief Security Commissioners of all Z onal Railways and all State Government 
Railway Police Chiefs in September, 1996 to  discuss the strategy to check crime on 
railways. Further a joint 
meeting was held in August, 1998 attended by the then Minister for Railways (MR.). 
The M.R. also convened a meeting of Chie f Secretaries and Directors General/Police 
of all State Governments and RPF officials in January, 2000. 
Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2000] 
Based on the Action Plan and discussion in the joint meeting, following action has 
been taken:— 
(1) Lodging of FIR has been made easier and victim friendly. 
(2) Investigation of pending cases is being expendited by the GRP authorities. 
(3) Special raids are being conducted by the GRP against absconding accused. 
(4) Mobile Police Posts have been opened in few selected trains. 
(5) Police>RPF booths have been provided on platforms for the assistance of 
passengers. 
(6) As   far   as   possible   trains   are   escorted   by   GRP   in   the vulnerable 
section specially during night hours. 
(7) The compendium of criminals operating on railways are being prepared for 
sharing of criminal intelligence. 
(8) Special joint drives are being conducted against undesirable elements in the 
Station area. 
(9) Periodical coordination meetings between RPF and GRP are being 
conducted regularly. 
(10) Steps for modernization of RPF have been initiated.

Increase In Rail Accidents 
tl526. SHRI SURYABHAN PATIL VAH ADANE: Will the Minister of 
RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Governments reaction to the news item captioned "Bharat Main rail 
durghatnain bharhi", published in Punjab Kesari dated 4th July, 2000 and whether 
Government are contemplating to take any concrete steps in this regard; and 
(b) if so, what are the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI 
DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) and (b) The universally accepted index of train accidents 
is number of train accidents per million kilometres. This index which stood at 5.5. in 
1960-61 has come down to 0.58 consequential train accidents per million train 
kilometres during the years 1997-98 and 1998-99. On Indian Railways, 
approximately 65 to 70% accidents are due to Railway staff failure. Railways 
accord the highest priority to the safe ty aspect and constantly endeavour to 
prevent train accidents. 
Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2000) 
Some of the important steps being taken to prevent accidents are listed below: 
(i) The work of track circuiting has been accelerated on the trunk routes and 
other important main lines. 
(ii) Modification of the signalling circ uitry is being carried out to minimise 
chances of human error in causing accidents. 
(iii) Walkie-Talkie sets have been supplied to Drivers and Guards of all trains. 
(iv) There has been progressive increase in use of Tie Tamping and ballast 
cleaning machines for track maintenance. 
(v) For monitoring track geometry and running characteristics 
of the track, sophisticated track recording cars, oscillograph cars and 
portable accelerometers are being progressively used. 
(vi) For detecting rail fractures and we ld failures, 96 more double rail Ultra 
Sonic Flaw Detectors are being procured. 
(vii) Maintenance facilities for coaches and wagons have been modernised and 
upgraded at many depots. 
(viii) To prevent cases of cold breakage of exles, Routine Over Hauling Depots 
have been equipped with ultrasonic testing equipment for detection of 
flaws in the exles. 
(ix) Whistle boards/speed breakers and road signs have been provided  at  
unmanned  level crossing and visibility  for 
drivers has been improved. 
(x) Periodic Safety Audit of different divisions by interdisciplinary teams 
from zonal headquarters has been introduced. 
(xi) Training facilities for drivers, guards and staff connected with train 
operation have been modernised inlcuding use of Simulators for training 
of drivers. 
(xii) Refresher courses are regularly organised at specified intervals. 
164 

[4 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(xiii) Performance of the staff connected with train operation is being constantly 
monitored and those found deficient are sent for attending crash courses. 
(xiv) Periodical safety drives are launched to inculcate, safety consciousness 
among the staff.

Within the above mentioned broad frame work, the Science & Technology policy 
and programme are continually reviewed and updated for implementation so as to 
adjust to the developments and trends in Science & Technology world over as well as 
the short term, medium term and long term national interests.

AIDS, as the biggest kilter in India 
SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE (Assam): Sir, I would like to refer 
to the latest report of UNICEF on the pr ogress of nations, that as many as 
3,40,000 men and 5,70,000 women in India are infected with HIV-AIDS virus, 
the second largest in the world. All of  them are in the age group of 15-24 
years. The number goes up by anot her 2.50,000, if children and elderly 
persons   affected   by   the   disease are taken into consideration.

RAJYA SABHA (4 August, 2000] 
The same report also says that 28 per cent of Indian women who become 
mothers by the age of 18 years are infected with this virus. And this statistics 
is only about the cases reported. A ccording to the UNICEF report, for every 
case that is reported, t here are at least two cases which are not reported for 
being ostracized by the society. 
In view of these facts, I would urge upon the Government to draw up, 
immediately, a time bound action plan for eradication of this deadly disease 
from the country and for giving the widest possible publicity through press, 
T.V. and other public media, creating a social awareness among the people 
about the name of the disease, its prevention and cure. 
Floods In Arunachal Pradesh 
SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN (Karnataka): Mr. Chairman, Sir, it is reported 
that, last month, a dam in Tibet has breached, causing floods in Arunachal 
Pradesh, which claimed 30 lives. More than 100 tribals are missing, according 
to the official sources from the Arunachal Pradesh Government. The Tsango 
River, which originates in China flows into India and is called 'Siang' in 
Arunachal Pradesh, and 'Brahmaputra' in  Assam. More than 50,000 people in 
five districts of Arunachal Pradesh have been rendered homeless by the 
floods, while several parts of the State were cut off from the rest of the 
country. More than 20 big bridges, a lifeline for the people, have been washed 
away by strong currents. Even today, most of the villagers are taking shelter in 
temporary camps and huts. The loss is esti mated at 100 crores of rupees, It 
will take years for the areas, hit by the floods, to regain the original status. 
Arunachal Pradesh is a small State and a sensitive border St ate, it has no 
resources to meet such an unprecedented situation. It is obligatory on the 
part of the Central Government to rush aid to Arunachal Pradesh and sanction 
urgent funds for rehabilitat ion. The Central Government should not follow its 
usual time-consuming procedure to give aid. Instead, the Central Government 
should rush aid immediately. I dem and a statement from  the Government 
stating as to what action has been taken and how much relief has been given 
so far.

Distress Sale Of Paddy In Orissa 
DR. M, N. DAS (Orissa): Sir, this special mention is regarding the distress 
sale of paddy in Orissa. The super cyclone of October, 1999 rendered more 
than a million people homeless, destroye d lakhs of cattle .and inundated 
agricultural lands.with saline water. Ye t, the hapless farmers, faced with stark 
starvation, worked hard to raise high-yield crops like taichung and irate and 
did succeed. They purchased bullocks and fertilizers and hired labourers at a 
high wage. For such an investment they borrowed heavy   amounts of money.   
The investment resulted in excellent harvest. 
193 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August. 2000) 
But the poor and marginal farmers are now forced to go in for distress sale of 
paddy to pay back the loans. The cost of  cultivation per acre, on an average, 
comes to Rs.6,000 to Rs.6,500 due to rise in the prices of diesel, kerosene, 
fertilizers and pesticides. Yield per acre roughly comes to 15 quintals. The 
present rate of distress sale price per quintal being Rs.350 to Rs.370 only, the 
peasants suffer a loss of Rs. 1.250 per acre for cultivating the land, The 
Government does not purchase paddy at  the • support price of Rs,490 for 
common paddy and Rs.520 for fine paddy for lack of storage system. The 
season for monsoon cultivation having approached, peasants have no 
economic means to cultivate their fields. If the crop is not raised and harvest 
does not yield usual quantit y of paddy, the future of the peasantry will turn 
bleak. I request the Government to take timely steps.  Otherwise, Orissa will 
face a famine-like situation. 
Leasing of Airports and implementation of Airports Authority 
Of India Act. 1994. 
SHRI R. MARGABANDU (Tamil Nadu):   Sir, the subject of my special 
mention is leasing of airports and impl ementation of the Airports Authority of 
India Act, 1994. 
Sir, the recent decision of the Cabine t Committee to go in for a long-term 
lease of five airports to the private sector is causing concern because it will 
lead to a huge loss to the exchequer and the security of our nation will be at 
stake. This move will result in the revenue loss of Rs.130 crores per year. 
Thirteen airports have a combined profit of Rs.400 crores and 107 airports 
suffer a loss of Rs.83 crores. The Airports Authority of India is. the only 
organisation making profit in the civil aviation industry. To overcome this loss of 
Rs.83 crores, Alports Authority of India Act, 1994 was passed to merge 
international and national divisions and to  bring it under one authority, that is, 
AAI, for the development of all airports. 
The merger of both the divisions has not yet been implemented. Instead, 
the Government is going opposite by clearing the decks in favour of long-term 
lease to enable the Indian airports to attain global standards. World-class 
facilities should not be compromised at the cost of national security. 
Furthermore, the wage revision for the employees in the officers cadre has 
been implemented with retrospective effect, while the Group C and D 
employees are staging demonstrations and dharnas for its implementation In 
the negotiations between the managemen t and the workers, the management 
has agreed to pay an advance amount to Group

C and D employees. But til! now no official order has been issued as per the 
agreement. So. justice should be done immediately to the Group C and D 
employees. I urge upon the Government to stop the process of leasing out the 
airports and immediately implement the Ai rports Authority of India Act, 1994.  
Thank you.

National Agricultural Insurance Scheme 
SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA RADDY (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, the 
Government of Andhra Pradesh has started implementing the National 
Agricultural insurance Scheme from Kharif 2000 onwards. As per the 
guidelines of the Scheme, the cut-off date for payment of premium and 
enrolment of non-loanee farmers is gi ven as one month after sowing/planting 
or 31st July, whichever is earlier. This stipulation is causing inconvenience to 
the non-loanee farmers as most of the rainfed crops in Andhra Pradesh will be 
continued to be sown even beyond the months of July and August. After 
thorough discussion in the SLCC meeting and considering the time of sowing 
of different crops in different districts,  the cut-off dates for loanee farmers are 
fixed ranging from the end of September to end of December. In this regard, f 
submit that when the cut-off dates be yond 31st July are fixed for loanee 
farmers, it would be appropriate to adopt the same method for the non-loanee 
farmers as well so that many non-loan ee farmers can become stakeholders in 
the new Scheme. Hence, I request the Mini stry of Agriculture to consider the 
special circumstances prevailing in Andhra Pradesh and permission may be 
accorded to keep the cut-off dates for non-loanee farmers on par with the 
loanee farmers so that uniformity in cut-off dates for different crops grown in 
the State can be maintained, which, I am sure, would attract more non-loanee 
farmers under the scheme. Thank you.
